content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines for the treatment of Treponema pallidum (syphilis). These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for drug therapy in managing syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. The publication emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material do not imply any legal or territorial opinions by WHO, nor do they endorse specific companies or products over others of a similar nature. Proprietary product names are distinguished by initial capital letters. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information in this publication. However, the material is distributed without any warranty, expressed or implied. The responsibility for interpreting and using the material lies with the reader, and WHO is not liable for any damages arising from its use. The guidelines were developed with input from a diverse group of experts from various regions and institutions. For example: Dr. Yaw Adu-Sarkodie from Ghana, affiliated with the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Andrew Amato from Sweden, representing the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, also declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. John Changalucha from Tanzania disclosed prior research support from GSK to evaluate HPV vaccine safety and immunogenicity, though this was unrelated to syphilis guidelines. Dr. Craig Cohen from the USA declared involvement in consulting for the development of new drugs for bacterial vaginosis, unrelated to syphilis treatment. Dr. Suzanne Garland from Australia disclosed financial support from various organizations, including Merck, GSK, and CSL Bio, for HPV-related research and trials, which were not directly related to syphilis treatment. Other contributors, such as Dr. Nicola Low from Switzerland, Dr. David Mabey from the United Kingdom, and Dr. Magnus Unemo from Sweden, declared no conflicts of interest. Similarly, experts like Dr. Jeffrey Klausner from the USA disclosed receiving free STI tests and travel support from diagnostic companies, though these were unrelated to syphilis treatment recommendations.
